suggestions.quote: I'll forget it all after anyway
suggestions.fix: Tag the voice direction: dry, tired, half-muttered, the way you say it every exam night. Keep the contraction and let it trail off, 'I'll forget it all after anyway…', so the later 'Forgetting is losing' has something to turn against.

Direction: flat, certain, a little proud, because the script has to break this line at the turn. Give it its own take with a short beat before it, and keep the wording identical when it is broken in the third jump.

suggestions.quote: you remember both; which one gets the last word tonight?
suggestions.fix: Split it into a spoken pair: 'You remember both. Which one gets the last word tonight?' Direction: hushed, then curious. The figure answers at once by reaching for the tea, so no held pause.

suggestions.quote: one sourced finding on recall against understanding
suggestions.fix: Write the finding as a spoken fragment with its answer right behind it: 'The question wants a page you've never read. You freeze. Why?' Then one plain sentence for the fact, with no abbreviation or study name aloud. Direction: surprised, then dry.

suggestions.quote: people who remember almost every day of their lives
suggestions.fix: Add to say.yaml: 'highly superior autobiographical memory' is never spoken. Use 'a memory that keeps almost every day'. Speak 'Jill Price' as 'jill price'. Study names (Parker, Cahill and McGaugh; LePort) go in the description, not the voice, and years such as 2006 or 2017 are not read aloud.

suggestions.quote: You repeat mom's exact words from years ago, expecting her to remember and say sorry; she genuinely remembers none of it
suggestions.fix: Say the blank in a fragment, not an explanation: 'You say it word for word. She looks at you. Nothing.' Direction: hushed, then wounded-quiet. Mom's words are a bubble of four words or fewer.

suggestions.quote: She doesn't remember the shout. You do. The tea's still warm.
suggestions.fix: Keep the contractions. Read 'You do.' as its own short take with a breath before it. Direction: warm, almost amused, dropping on 'warm'. The line must land as a full thought, which it does, so don't add a closing clause.
